summary:
Califire is an interactive web application that turns NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire detections into a comparable history of California’s burning activity. We developed a data-processing pipeline and website featuring daily and monthly calendars, interactive maps, historical comparisons, downloadable datasets, and experimental Timestral-5M forecasts.

The project addresses the challenge of combining observations from satellites with different detection capabilities. By harmonizing their measurements onto a common scale, Califire helps users distinguish changes in detected activity from changes caused by the sensors themselves. Users can select an area and date range to investigate local patterns across more than 25 years of observations.

Califire makes complex Earth-observation data accessible to students, researchers, educators, and communities. It supports understanding of fire seasonality and unusual activity while clearly communicating uncertainty, missing observations, and forecasting limitations.
details:
Califire is an interactive web application that makes California’s satellite-detected fire activity easier to explore and compare over time. Developed by Yashneil and Shrihan, it combines NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS into a harmonized record covering November 2000 through August 2026. These sensors detect different numbers of hotspots, so simply combining their raw counts can create misleading changes. Our Python pipeline cleans and filters the observations, organizes them geographically, and applies conversion factors learned from overlapping observations to produce a consistent MODIS-equivalent activity scale.

Users can explore daily and monthly burning calendars, view satellite detections on a map, compare activity with previous years, and download CSV files for further analysis. Drawing an area on the map applies that selection across the application, allowing users to investigate a specific part of California. The application also includes an experimental seven-day forecast using Mistral’s Timestral-5M model. It uses 730 days of harmonized daily counts to estimate future satellite-detected activity, displaying a median and a 10th–90th percentile range. Because the current archive ends in August 2026, the published forecast covers September 1–7, 2026.

The project’s intended impact is to make NASA’s open Earth-observation data more accessible to students, researchers, educators, and people studying regional fire patterns. Instead of requiring users to process large satellite datasets themselves, Califire provides a visual way to investigate seasonality, unusual activity, and historical differences. Its creativity comes from connecting sensor harmonization, linked geographic exploration, historical comparisons, and lightweight forecasting in one transparent application.

We developed the data pipeline in Python using tools including pandas, NumPy, and PyArrow. The website uses TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre GL, with NASA GIBS imagery as its map background. Timestral inference runs through PyTorch, while GitHub Actions automates forecasting and GitHub Pages hosts the website. CPU inference allows the forecasting component to run without specialized GPU hardware.

Our team considered sensor differences, double counting, satellite outages, performance, accessibility, reproducibility, and uncertainty. Missing observations remain missing rather than being treated as zero activity. We also evaluated forecasts against seasonal and persistence baselines and reported their limitations: Timestral performed better than the seasonal baseline overall but did not outperform simply repeating the last observation, and it underestimated the busiest days. Califire therefore supports exploration and research; its hotspot counts and experimental forecasts do not represent individual fires, burned area, or emergency guidance.
